# num_order - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-order/

## Expand description

`num-order` implements numerically consistent [Eq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Eq.html), [Ord](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html) and
[Hash](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.Hash.html) for various `num` types.

```
use std::cmp::Ordering;
use std::hash::Hasher;
use std::collections::hash_map::DefaultHasher;
use num_order::NumOrd;
assert!(NumOrd::num_eq(&3u64, &3.0f32));
assert!(NumOrd::num_lt(&-4.7f64, &-4i8));
assert!(!NumOrd::num_ge(&-3i8, &1u16));
// 40_000_000 can be exactly represented in f32, 40_000_001 cannot
// 40_000_001 becames 40_000_000.0 in f32
assert_eq!(NumOrd::num_cmp(&40_000_000f32, &40_000_000u32), Ordering::Equal);
assert_ne!(NumOrd::num_cmp(&40_000_001f32, &40_000_001u32), Ordering::Equal);
assert_eq!(NumOrd::num_partial_cmp(&f32::NAN, &40_000_002u32), None);
use num_order::NumHash;
// same hash values are guaranteed for equal numbers
let mut hasher1 = DefaultHasher::new();
3u64.num_hash(&mut hasher1);
let mut hasher2 = DefaultHasher::new();
3.0f32.num_hash(&mut hasher2);
assert_eq!(hasher1.finish(), hasher2.finish())
```
This crate can serve applications where [float-ord](https://crates.io/crates/float-ord),
[num-cmp](https://crates.io/crates/num-cmp), [num-ord](https://crates.io/crates/num-ord) are used.
Meanwhile it also supports hashing and more numeric types (`num-bigint`, etc.).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional Features

- `std`: enable std library
- `num-bigint`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-bigint::{BigInt, BigUint}`
- `num-rational`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-rational::Ratio<I>`, where- `I`can be- `i8`,- `i16`,- `i32`,- `i64`,- `i128`and- `isize`.- `Ratio<BigInt>`is supported when both- `num-bigint`and- `num-rational`is enabled
- `num-complex`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-complex::{Complex32, Complex64}`

---

# num_order - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-order/1.2.0/num_order/

## Expand description

`num-order` implements numerically consistent [Eq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Eq.html), [Ord](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html) and
[Hash](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.Hash.html) for various `num` types.

```
use std::cmp::Ordering;
use std::hash::Hasher;
use std::collections::hash_map::DefaultHasher;
use num_order::NumOrd;
assert!(NumOrd::num_eq(&3u64, &3.0f32));
assert!(NumOrd::num_lt(&-4.7f64, &-4i8));
assert!(!NumOrd::num_ge(&-3i8, &1u16));
// 40_000_000 can be exactly represented in f32, 40_000_001 cannot
// 40_000_001 becames 40_000_000.0 in f32
assert_eq!(NumOrd::num_cmp(&40_000_000f32, &40_000_000u32), Ordering::Equal);
assert_ne!(NumOrd::num_cmp(&40_000_001f32, &40_000_001u32), Ordering::Equal);
assert_eq!(NumOrd::num_partial_cmp(&f32::NAN, &40_000_002u32), None);
use num_order::NumHash;
// same hash values are guaranteed for equal numbers
let mut hasher1 = DefaultHasher::new();
3u64.num_hash(&mut hasher1);
let mut hasher2 = DefaultHasher::new();
3.0f32.num_hash(&mut hasher2);
assert_eq!(hasher1.finish(), hasher2.finish())
```
This crate can serve applications where [float-ord](https://crates.io/crates/float-ord),
[num-cmp](https://crates.io/crates/num-cmp), [num-ord](https://crates.io/crates/num-ord) are used.
Meanwhile it also supports hashing and more numeric types (`num-bigint`, etc.).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional Features

- `std`: enable std library
- `num-bigint`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-bigint::{BigInt, BigUint}`
- `num-rational`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-rational::Ratio<I>`, where- `I`can be- `i8`,- `i16`,- `i32`,- `i64`,- `i128`and- `isize`.- `Ratio<BigInt>`is supported when both- `num-bigint`and- `num-rational`is enabled
- `num-complex`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-complex::{Complex32, Complex64}`

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-order/latest

Numerically consistent `Eq`, `Ord` and `Hash` implementations for various `num` types (`u32`, `f64`, `num_bigint::BigInt`, etc.).

# Example

```
use Ordering;
use Hasher;
use DefaultHasher;
use ;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// 40_000_000 can be exactly represented in f32, 40_000_001 cannot
// 40_000_001 becames 40_000_000.0 in f32
assert_eq!;
assert_ne!;
assert_eq!;
// same hash values are guaranteed for equal numbers
let mut hasher1 = new;
3u64.num_hash;
let mut hasher2 = new;
3.0f32.num_hash;
assert_eq!
```

# num_bigint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-bigint/^0.4.0/

## Expand description

Big Integer Types for Rust

- A `BigUint`
- A `BigInt``BigUint``Sign`

Common numerical operations are overloaded, so we can treat them the same way we treat other numbers.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use num_bigint::BigUint;
use num_traits::One;
// Calculate large fibonacci numbers.
fn fib(n: usize) -> BigUint {
    let mut f0 = BigUint::ZERO;
    let mut f1 = BigUint::ONE;
    for _ in 0..n {
        let f2 = f0 + &f1;
        f0 = f1;
        f1 = f2;
    }
    f0
}
// This is a very large number.
println!("fib(1000) = {}", fib(1000));
```
It’s easy to generate large random numbers:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use num_bigint::{ToBigInt, RandBigInt};
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let a = rng.gen_bigint(1000);
let low = -10000.to_bigint().unwrap();
let high = 10000.to_bigint().unwrap();
let b = rng.gen_bigint_range(&low, &high);
// Probably an even larger number.
println!("{}", a * b);
```
See the “Features” section for instructions for enabling random number generation.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

The `std` crate feature is enabled by default, which enables [ std::error::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html)
implementations and some internal use of floating point approximations. This can be disabled by
depending on

`num-bigint` with `default-features = false`. Either way, the `alloc` crate is
always required for heap allocation of the [/](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[digits.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#random-generation)Random Generation

`num-bigint` supports the generation of random big integers when the `rand`
feature is enabled. To enable it include rand as

```
rand = "0.8"
num-bigint = { version = "0.4", features = ["rand"] }
```
Note that you must use the version of `rand` that `num-bigint` is compatible
with: `0.8`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arbitrary-big-integers)Arbitrary Big Integers

`num-bigint` supports `arbitrary` and `quickcheck` features to implement
[ arbitrary::Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/arbitrary/1.4.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html) and

[, respectively, for both](https://docs.rs/quickcheck/1.0.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/quickcheck/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`quickcheck::Arbitrary`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[. These are useful for fuzzing and other forms of randomized testing.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#serialization)Serialization

The `serde` feature adds implementations of [ Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html) and

[for both](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)

`Deserialize`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[. Their serialized data is generated portably, regardless of platform differences like the internal digit size.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

The `num-bigint` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)
- A big signed integer type.
- [BigUint](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)
- A big unsigned integer type.
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/struct.ParseBigIntError.html)- BigInt - Error

- A random distribution for `BigUint``BigInt`

- The error type returned when a checked conversion regarding big integer fails.
- [U32Digits](https://docs.rs/struct.U32Digits.html)
- An iterator of `u32`digits representation of a`BigUint``BigInt`
- [U64Digits](https://docs.rs/struct.U64Digits.html)
- An iterator of `u64`digits representation of a`BigUint``BigInt`
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformBigInt.html)- BigInt - `rand`
- The back-end implementing rand’s `UniformSampler``BigInt`
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformBigUint.html)- BigUint - `rand`
- The back-end implementing rand’s `UniformSampler``BigUint`

# num_modular - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-modular/^0.6.1/

## Expand description

This crate provides efficient Modular arithmetic operations for various integer types,
including primitive integers and `num-bigint`. The latter option is enabled optionally.

To achieve fast modular arithmetics, convert integers to any [ModularInteger](https://docs.rs/trait.ModularInteger.html) implementation
use static `new()` or associated [ModularInteger::convert()](https://docs.rs/trait.ModularInteger.html#tymethod.convert) functions. Some builtin implementations
of [ModularInteger](https://docs.rs/trait.ModularInteger.html) includes [MontgomeryInt](https://docs.rs/type.MontgomeryInt.html), [FixedMersenneInt](https://docs.rs/type.FixedMersenneInt.html) and [FixedSolinasInt](https://docs.rs/type.FixedSolinasInt.html).

Example code:

```
use num_modular::{ModularCoreOps, ModularInteger, MontgomeryInt};
// directly using methods in ModularCoreOps
let (x, y, m) = (12u8, 13u8, 5u8);
assert_eq!(x.mulm(y, &m), x * y % m);
// convert integers into ModularInteger
let mx = MontgomeryInt::new(x, &m);
let my = mx.convert(y); // faster than static MontgomeryInt::new(y, m)
assert_eq!((mx * my).residue(), x * y % m);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#comparison-of-fast-division--modular-arithmetics)Comparison of fast division / modular arithmetics

Several fast division / modulo tricks are provided in these crate, the difference of them are listed below:

- [PreModInv](https://docs.rs/struct.PreModInv.html): pre-compute modular inverse of the divisor, only applicable to exact division
- Barrett (to be implemented): pre-compute (rational approximation of) the reciprocal of the divisor, applicable to fast division and modulo
- [Montgomery](https://docs.rs/struct.Montgomery.html): Convert the dividend into a special form by shifting and pre-compute a modular inverse, only applicable to fast modulo, but faster than Barrett reduction
- [FixedMersenne](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedMersenne.html): Specialization of modulo in form- `2^P-K`under 2^127.
- [FixedTrinomialSolinas](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedTrinomialSolinas.html): Specialization of modulo in form- `2^P1-2^P2+K`under 2^127.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_fixed_monty_ops.html)- fixed_ - monty_ - ops
- Generates all `Reducer`methods except`new()`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedMersenne.html)- Mersenne
- A modular reducer for (pseudo) Mersenne numbers `2^P - K`as modulus.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedMersenne32.html)- Mersenne32
- A modular reducer for (pseudo) Mersenne numbers `2^P - K`as modulus with 32-bit operands.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedMersenne64.html)- Mersenne64
- A modular reducer for (pseudo) Mersenne numbers `2^P - K`as modulus with 64-bit operands.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedMontgomery32.html)- Montgomery32
- A modular reducer based on [Montgomery form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_modular_multiplication#Montgomery_form)for 32-bit operands, with the modulus`P`known at compile time.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedMontgomery64.html)- Montgomery64
- A modular reducer based on [Montgomery form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_modular_multiplication#Montgomery_form)for 64-bit operands, with the modulus`P`known at compile time.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedProth.html)- Proth
- A modular reducer for Proth primes `K * 2^N + 1`.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedProth32.html)- Proth32
- A modular reducer for Proth primes `K * 2^N + 1`with 32-bit operands.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedProth64.html)- Proth64
- A modular reducer for Proth primes `K * 2^N + 1`with 64-bit operands.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedTrinomialSolinas.html)- Trinomial - Solinas
- A modular reducer for trinomial Solinas numbers `2^P1 - 2^P2 + K`as modulus.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedTrinomialSolinas32.html)- Trinomial - Solinas32
- A modular reducer for trinomial Solinas numbers `2^P1 - 2^P2 + K`as modulus with 32-bit operands.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedTrinomialSolinas64.html)- Trinomial - Solinas64
- A modular reducer for trinomial Solinas numbers `2^P1 - 2^P2 + K`as modulus with 64-bit operands.
- [Montgomery](https://docs.rs/struct.Montgomery.html)
- A modular reducer based on [Montgomery form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_modular_multiplication#Montgomery_form), only supports odd modulus.
- [Normalized2by1](https://docs.rs/struct.Normalized2by1Divisor.html)- Divisor
- Divide a DoubleWord by a prearranged divisor.
- [Normalized3by2](https://docs.rs/struct.Normalized3by2Divisor.html)- Divisor
- Divide a 3-Word by a prearranged DoubleWord divisor.
- [PreMod](https://docs.rs/struct.PreModInv.html)- Inv
- Pre-computing the modular inverse for fast divisibility check.
- [PreMul](https://docs.rs/struct.PreMulInv1by1.html)- Inv1by1
- Divide a Word by a prearranged divisor.
- [PreMul](https://docs.rs/struct.PreMulInv2by1.html)- Inv2by1
- A wrapper of [Normalized2by1Divisor](https://docs.rs/struct.Normalized2by1Divisor.html)that can be used as a[Reducer](https://docs.rs/trait.Reducer.html)
- [PreMul](https://docs.rs/struct.PreMulInv3by2.html)- Inv3by2
- A wrapper of [Normalized3by2Divisor](https://docs.rs/struct.Normalized3by2Divisor.html)that can be used as a[Reducer](https://docs.rs/trait.Reducer.html)
- [Reduced](https://docs.rs/struct.ReducedInt.html)- Int
- An integer in a modulo ring
- [Vanilla](https://docs.rs/struct.Vanilla.html)
- A plain reducer that just use normal [Rem](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.Rem.html)operators. It will keep the integer in range [0, modulus) after each operation.
- [udouble](https://docs.rs/struct.udouble.html)
- A double width integer type based on the largest built-in integer type [umax](https://docs.rs/type.umax.html)(currently[u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u128.html)), and to support double-width operations on it is the only goal for this type.

- Modular power functions

- Collection of operations similar to [ModularOps](https://docs.rs/trait.ModularOps.html), but takes operands with references
- [Modular](https://docs.rs/trait.ModularSymbols.html)- Symbols
- Math symbols related to modular arithmetics
- [Modular](https://docs.rs/trait.ModularUnaryOps.html)- Unary - Ops
- Core unary modular arithmetics
- [Reducer](https://docs.rs/trait.Reducer.html)
- A modular reducer that can ensure that the operations on integers are all performed in a modular ring.

- [Num](https://docs.rs/trait.Num.html)
- The base trait for numeric types, covering `0`and`1`values, comparisons, basic numeric operations, and string conversion.
- [NumAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.NumAssign.html)
- The trait for `Num`types which also implement assignment operators.

- Generic trait for types implementing numeric assignment operators (like `+=`).
- [NumAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.NumAssignRef.html)- Ref
- The trait for `NumAssign`types which also implement assignment operations taking the second operand by reference.
- [NumOps](https://docs.rs/trait.NumOps.html)
- Generic trait for types implementing basic numeric operations
- [NumRef](https://docs.rs/trait.NumRef.html)
- The trait for `Num`types which also implement numeric operations taking the second operand by reference.
- [RefNum](https://docs.rs/trait.RefNum.html)
- The trait for `Num`references which implement numeric operations, taking the second operand either by value or by reference.

# num_order - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-order/latest/target-redirect/num_order/

## Expand description

`num-order` implements numerically consistent [Eq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Eq.html), [Ord](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html) and
[Hash](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.Hash.html) for various `num` types.

```
use std::cmp::Ordering;
use std::hash::Hasher;
use std::collections::hash_map::DefaultHasher;
use num_order::NumOrd;
assert!(NumOrd::num_eq(&3u64, &3.0f32));
assert!(NumOrd::num_lt(&-4.7f64, &-4i8));
assert!(!NumOrd::num_ge(&-3i8, &1u16));
// 40_000_000 can be exactly represented in f32, 40_000_001 cannot
// 40_000_001 becames 40_000_000.0 in f32
assert_eq!(NumOrd::num_cmp(&40_000_000f32, &40_000_000u32), Ordering::Equal);
assert_ne!(NumOrd::num_cmp(&40_000_001f32, &40_000_001u32), Ordering::Equal);
assert_eq!(NumOrd::num_partial_cmp(&f32::NAN, &40_000_002u32), None);
use num_order::NumHash;
// same hash values are guaranteed for equal numbers
let mut hasher1 = DefaultHasher::new();
3u64.num_hash(&mut hasher1);
let mut hasher2 = DefaultHasher::new();
3.0f32.num_hash(&mut hasher2);
assert_eq!(hasher1.finish(), hasher2.finish())
```
This crate can serve applications where [float-ord](https://crates.io/crates/float-ord),
[num-cmp](https://crates.io/crates/num-cmp), [num-ord](https://crates.io/crates/num-ord) are used.
Meanwhile it also supports hashing and more numeric types (`num-bigint`, etc.).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional Features

- `std`: enable std library
- `num-bigint`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-bigint::{BigInt, BigUint}`
- `num-rational`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-rational::Ratio<I>`, where- `I`can be- `i8`,- `i16`,- `i32`,- `i64`,- `i128`and- `isize`.- `Ratio<BigInt>`is supported when both- `num-bigint`and- `num-rational`is enabled
- `num-complex`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-complex::{Complex32, Complex64}`

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# bevy_3d_tiles - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bevy_3d_tiles/0.1.1/bevy_3d_tiles/

## Expand description

3D Tiles 1.1 streaming plugin (BEVY-3D-TILES-PLAN, phases T0/T1).

One traversal engine for tiled meshes (T0/T1), point clouds (T2), and splats (T3) — the generalization of the basemap streamer’s proven selection/fetch machinery from quadtree arithmetic to tileset-defined trees (plan D5):

- `schema`- `tileset.json`serde model.
- `archive`- `.3tz`ranged reader (tail-scan →- `@3dtilesIndex1@`→ two range-GETs per entry; D2’s one-blob-per-asset artifact).
- `traversal`
- `fetch`
- `content`
- this module — ECS wiring: per-frame selection, the request scheduler (priorities recomputed each frame, out-of-cut requests aborted), time-boxed content spawning, visibility cut, eviction, and the attach/detach surface the asset loader drives (D6).

**Anchoring (T1)**: a tileset attaches to an *anchor entity* — the twin
entity (ENU placement + per-frame twin transform) or a preview root. The
tileset’s root entity is parented under the anchor with the rendition
correction as its local transform, so tiles inherit world placement the
exact way whole-file scenes do. Selection math runs in the tileset’s local
frame: the camera is pulled into that frame per set, which keeps SSE exact
under rigid/uniform anchor transforms without rebuilding tree volumes.
Dev-trigger tilesets (`TT_TILES3D=…` / `?tiles3d=…`) stay world-anchored.

[§](https://docs.rs#error-convention-public-sdk-surface)Error convention (public SDK surface)

Public fallible APIs return `thiserror` types, never `String`/`anyhow`:
[ fetch::FetchError](https://docs.rs/fetch/enum.FetchError.html) (with cancellation as the distinct

[variant — callers treat an abort differently from a failure),](https://docs.rs/fetch/enum.FetchError.html#variant.Aborted)

`fetch::FetchError::Aborted`[, and](https://docs.rs/archive/enum.ArchiveError.html)

`archive::ArchiveError`[(staged: permanent content failures vs environmental transcoder-shim failures). Internal helpers may pass plain](https://docs.rs/content/struct.DecodeError.html)

`content::DecodeError``String` messages; the typed boundary is the public function signature.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use api::`- [PointTileMaterial](https://docs.rs/api/struct.PointTileMaterial.html);
- `pub use api::`- [EcefOrigin](https://docs.rs/api/struct.EcefOrigin.html);
- `pub use api::`- [TileFeatureResolver](https://docs.rs/api/struct.TileFeatureResolver.html);
- `pub use api::`- [TileOwner](https://docs.rs/api/struct.TileOwner.html);
- `pub use api::`- [Tiles3dCamera](https://docs.rs/api/struct.Tiles3dCamera.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [api](https://docs.rs/api/index.html)
- Public, backend-agnostic API surface for `bevy_3d_tiles`.
- [archive](https://docs.rs/archive/index.html)
- `.3tz`ranged reader (BEVY-3D-TILES-PLAN T0, decision D2).
- [content](https://docs.rs/content/index.html)
- Tile content decode: GLB bytes → renderable data for the three content
types (plan D5) — triangle meshes (T0/T1), point clouds (T2), Gaussian
splats (T3). One decoder, three outputs, feeding the existing renderers
(`Mesh3d`, vendored`PointCloud`,`PlanarGaussian3d`).
- [draco](https://docs.rs/draco/index.html)
- Platform Draco decode for `KHR_draco_mesh_compression`tile content (BEVY-3D-TILES T4 — Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles ship Draco-compressed meshes; no published pure-Rust decoder exists yet, 2026-06 survey).
- [fetch](https://docs.rs/fetch/index.html)
- Byte-source IO for 3D Tiles content (BEVY-3D-TILES-PLAN T0).
- [geo](https://docs.rs/geo/index.html)
- Georeferenced-tileset geometry (BEVY-3D-TILES T4).
- [geodesy](https://docs.rs/geodesy/index.html)
- Minimal WGS84 geodesy — the only math `bevy_3d_tiles`needs to georeference ECEF/region tilesets. Pure textbook formulas (no external crate, no STDB dependency); inlined from TurboTwin’s`turbotwin_sdk_rs::enu`so the crate is self-contained. Besides geodetic→ECEF and the radius constant used in horizon culling,`world_from_ecef``crate::EcefOrigin`
- [meshopt](https://docs.rs/meshopt/index.html)
- Pure-Rust `EXT_meshopt_compression`decoder for tile content (BEVY-3D-TILES T6, decision D12 — we EMIT meshopt, never Draco, and decode it on the CPU).
- [schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)
- Serde model for 3D Tiles 1.1 `tileset.json`(BEVY-3D-TILES-PLAN T0).
- [traversal](https://docs.rs/traversal/index.html)
- Tile-tree model + the per-frame selection algorithm (BEVY-3D-TILES-PLAN §7).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Active](https://docs.rs/struct.ActiveTileset.html)- Tileset
- One streaming tileset.
- [P3dt](https://docs.rs/struct.P3dtParams.html)- Params
- Google P3DT per-layer config, denormalized from the project row (L3).
- [Tiles3d](https://docs.rs/struct.Tiles3dAttach.html)- Attach
- Attach a streaming tileset under an anchor entity (D6 resolver routing —
sent by the asset loader for `"3dtiles"`renditions, and by the layers resolver for world layers).
- [Tiles3d](https://docs.rs/struct.Tiles3dConfig.html)- Config
- [Tiles3d](https://docs.rs/struct.Tiles3dDetach.html)- Detach
- Tear down any tileset anchored to this entity (rebind / mode switch). Despawning the anchor outright works too — sets garbage-collect when their root entity dies with the hierarchy.
- [Tiles3d](https://docs.rs/struct.Tiles3dPlugin.html)- Plugin
- [Tiles3d](https://docs.rs/struct.Tiles3dSets.html)- Sets
- Live tilesets + scheduler counters.
- [Tiles3d](https://docs.rs/struct.Tiles3dTile.html)- Tile
- Marker on each spawned tile root entity.
- [Tileset](https://docs.rs/struct.TilesetCredits.html)- Credits
- Attribution side-band of the streaming tilesets, read by the basemap’s overlay system: aggregated tile copyrights (P3DT ToS requires showing them) and whether Google content is on screen (logo requirement).

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [GOOGLE_](https://docs.rs/constant.GOOGLE_P3DT_ROOT_URL.html)- P3DT_ - ROOT_ - URL
- The Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles root tileset (D7). The org’s API key is appended per request, never stored in the row.

# rsclaw-jobs 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rsclaw-jobs/0.1.0

Please check the

[build logs](https://docs.rs/crate/rsclaw-jobs/0.1.0/builds)for more information.

See

[Builds](https://docs.rs/about/builds)for ideas on how to fix a failed build, or

[Metadata](https://docs.rs/about/metadata)for how to configure docs.rs builds.

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).

`rsclaw-jobs` — pure provider-API job layer for async video / image
generation (crate-split, step-12 P2).

Lifted out of `gateway/external_jobs_worker.rs`: the per-provider HTTP
adapters (`submit_*` for the tool side, `poll_*` + `download_artifact`
for the worker side). This crate has NO gateway dependency — it knows
nothing about the task queue, `ExternalJob` persistence, channels, or
shutdown. The gateway-coupled `ExternalJobsWorker` tick/delivery loop
stays in root and calls back into these functions.

This breaks the old agent->gateway edge: `agent::tools_video` now calls
`rsclaw_jobs::submit_*` instead of reaching into the gateway worker.

Adding a new async provider means: add the corresponding `submit_*` for
the tool side and `poll_*` for the worker side, then extend the
`dispatch_poll` match in the gateway worker.

# hanzo-kernel 0.2.6 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/hanzo-kernel/0.2.6

Please check the

[build logs](https://docs.rs/crate/hanzo-kernel/0.2.6/builds)for more information.

See

[Builds](https://docs.rs/about/builds)for ideas on how to fix a failed build, or

[Metadata](https://docs.rs/about/metadata)for how to configure docs.rs builds.

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).

hanzo-kernel: Hanzo's first-party GPU kernel DSL.

Write a kernel ONCE in Rust; it lowers to CUDA / ROCm / Vulkan / Metal. This crate is the
first-party facade over the CubeCL lowering engine: kernel source names only `hanzo_kernel::*`,
never `cubecl`. "Values, not places" -- CubeCL is the implementation value; `hanzo_kernel` is the
stable namespace we build against, so the engine can be upgraded (or forked) without touching a
single kernel.

The perf primitives our hand-tuned kernels rely on are all here and lower to the native instruction on each backend:

- `dot`on a vectorized- `Line<i8>`-> dp4a / OpSDotAccSat (int8 4-way dot)
- `cmma`-> tensor cores (WMMA / cooperative-matrix / simdgroup)
- `SharedMemory`,- `plane_*`(subgroup reduce/shuffle),- `Atomic`, barriers

MIGRATION POLICY (perf-gated, never a downgrade): the DSL provides COVERAGE -- every quant type on every backend, from one source, killing the "same op, N impls, N numeric behaviors" bug class. A hand-tuned kernel is replaced by its DSL twin ONLY when the DSL version is bit-exact AND within perf noise (bench-gated). Where a hand-tuned kernel still wins, it stays as the specialized peak path and the DSL is the portable fallback for the backends that lack a tuned version.

# sim_lib_lang_scheme - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-lang-scheme/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_lang_scheme/

## Expand description

Scheme (R7RS-small) surface profile for the SIM runtime.

The kernel defines the codec, eval-policy, and `Expr` contracts; this crate
is a loadable language profile presenting a Scheme surface syntax over the
shared `Expr` graph, not a standalone interpreter.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Located](https://docs.rs/struct.LocatedSchemeLowering.html)- Scheme - Lowering
- A `SchemeLowered`
- [Scheme](https://docs.rs/struct.SchemeBaseExport.html)- Base - Export
- A Scheme base-library export: a surface symbol and its description.
- [Scheme](https://docs.rs/struct.SchemeCodec.html)- Codec
- Decoder turning Scheme surface text into the shared `Expr`graph.
- [Scheme](https://docs.rs/struct.SchemeCodecLib.html)- Codec - Lib
- Loadable `Lib``SchemeCodec`
- [Scheme](https://docs.rs/struct.SchemeFormSpec.html)- Form - Spec
- Specification of one R7RS-small surface form: its symbol, doc, match shape, and support status.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Scheme](https://docs.rs/enum.SchemeFormStatus.html)- Form - Status
- Whether a Scheme surface form is supported by this profile.
- [Scheme](https://docs.rs/enum.SchemeLowered.html)- Lowered
- Result of lowering a Scheme `Expr`to a runtime value.

- Lowers a located Scheme tree, preserving its origin.

- Parses one top-level Scheme form from source text into a located `Expr`tree.

# a3s 0.6.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/a3s/0.6.0

# a3s

The umbrella CLI for the [A3S](https://github.com/A3S-Lab) platform.

`a3s <tool> [args...]` runs the matching A3S tool. `a3s box ...` proxies to
`a3s-box ...` and bootstraps the Box runtime automatically if it is missing:

```
a3s code            # → a3s-code   (launches its TUI)
a3s box ps          # → a3s-box ps (auto-installs a3s-box if needed)
a3s <tool> --help   # a tool's own help
a3s list            # list installed a3s-* tools
a3s --version
```
## Install

```
# from source
# or from this repo
# or Homebrew
```
Then run the tools you need. `a3s box ...` installs `a3s-box` on first use.

## Account Models

In `a3s code`, `/model` lists configured `config.acl` models plus signed-in
account tabs. When Claude Code is logged in (`claude /login`), the Claude Code
tab can switch the current session to Claude models using the local Claude Code
OAuth credentials, including Claude Code's macOS Keychain entry.
`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` or `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` can also provide the account
token for non-standard environments. If Anthropic rejects the raw OAuth Messages
API bridge with a rate-limit or authentication error, a3s falls back to the
installed `claude` CLI in safe streaming mode; Claude Code's own tools stay
disabled while a3s host tools are requested through an adapter protocol and
still execute inside a3s-code. The adapter accepts Claude Code-style
`<function_calls>` output and tool names such as `Read` or `Bash`, normalizes
common argument aliases like `path` to a3s's `file_path`, and feeds tool results
back into the next Claude turn as structured history.

## Testing

```
```
The ignored soak test repeats `a3s box` after a fake first-use install and
verifies later runs reuse the installed `a3s-box`. The ignored
`ctx_compact_real_llm` test drives the configured model (`~/.a3s/config.acl`)
until the context crosses the auto-compact threshold and asserts streaming
usage is reported, compaction shrinks the history, and the next prompt drops —
the machinery behind the TUI's ctx%, fill warnings, and auto-compaction.

## Updating

In the TUI, ** /update** upgrades to the latest release and restarts into your
session — Homebrew installs are refreshed + upgraded; standalone installs swap
the binary directly. Both paths verify the installed binary reports the target
version before treating the update as successful.

If you're on an **older build (≤ 0.5.4)** whose `/update` was broken, it can't
upgrade itself, and `brew upgrade a3s` alone won't see the new version (Homebrew
doesn't re-sync a tap on `upgrade`). Bootstrap onto a current build once with:

```
 &&
```
From 0.5.5 onward, `/update` handles the tap refresh itself, so this manual step
isn't needed again.

## License

MIT

# a3s_code_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/a3s-code-core/4.2.9/a3s_code_core/

## Expand description

A3S Code Core Library

Harness-driven runtime for coding agents.

`Agent` and `AgentSession` are the primary 2.0 API. Lower-level session
runtime state is internal; persistence data flows through `store::SessionData`.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use a3s_code_core::{Agent, AgentEvent};
// From an ACL-compatible config file path (.acl)
let agent = Agent::new("agent.acl").await?;
// Create a workspace-bound session
let session = agent.session("/my-project", None)?;
// Non-streaming
let result = session.send("What files handle auth?", None).await?;
println!("{}", result.text);
// Streaming (AgentEvent is #[non_exhaustive])
let (mut rx, _handle) = session.stream("Refactor auth", None).await?;
while let Some(event) = rx.recv().await {
    match event {
        AgentEvent::TextDelta { text } => print!("{text}"),
        AgentEvent::End { .. } => break,
        _ => {} // required: #[non_exhaustive]
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#disposable-workers)Disposable Workers

```
use a3s_code_core::{Agent, SessionOptions, WorkerAgentSpec};
let agent = Agent::new("agent.acl").await?;
let frontend = WorkerAgentSpec::implementer(
    "frontend-cow",
    "Small verified frontend fixes",
)
.with_model_ref("openai/gpt-4o")
.with_max_steps(24);
let session = agent.session(
    "/my-project",
    Some(SessionOptions::new().with_worker_agent(frontend)),
)?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

```
Agent (config-driven facade)
  +-- AgentSession (workspace-bound execution API)
      +-- internal turn runner
      +-- ContextAssembler / ContextProvider
      +-- ToolSelector
      +-- ToolExecutor
      +-- ProgramExecutor (PTC)
      +-- SkillRegistry
      +-- Permission / confirmation
      +-- Trace / artifacts / verification evidence
Advanced infrastructure:
  +-- optional lane queues for explicit external/hybrid dispatch
```

# euv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/euv/0.8.15/euv/

## Expand description

euv

A declarative, cross-platform UI framework for Rust with virtual DOM, reactive signals, and HTML macros for WebAssembly.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [console_error_panic_hook](https://docs.rs/console_error_panic_hook/0.1.7/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/console_error_panic_hook/index.html);
- `pub use`- [js_sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys/0.3.103/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/js_sys/index.html);
- `pub use`- [wasm_bindgen](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/0.2.126/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen/index.html);
- `pub use`- [wasm_bindgen_futures](https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen-futures/0.4.76/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wasm_bindgen_futures/index.html);
- `pub use`- [web_sys](https://docs.rs/web-sys/0.3.103/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/web_sys/index.html);

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [class](https://docs.rs/macro.class.html)
- The `class!`macro for defining CSS classes with style properties.
- [computed](https://docs.rs/macro.computed.html)
- The `computed!`macro for creating reactive computed signals.
- [html](https://docs.rs/macro.html.html)
- The `html!`macro for writing declarative UI in euv.
- [var](https://docs.rs/macro.var.html)
- The `var!`macro for referencing CSS custom properties defined via`vars!`.
- [vars](https://docs.rs/macro.vars.html)
- The `vars!`macro for defining CSS custom properties.
- [watch](https://docs.rs/macro.watch.html)
- The `watch!`macro for creating reactive side effects.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Attr](https://docs.rs/struct.AttrValueAdapter.html)- Value - Adapter
- Adapts an arbitrary attribute value expression into an `AttributeValue`.
- [Attribute](https://docs.rs/struct.AttributeEntry.html)- Entry
- Represents a single attribute on a virtual DOM node.
- [Callback](https://docs.rs/struct.CallbackNamedAdapter.html)- Named - Adapter
- Adapts a callback with a custom name into an `AttributeValue`.
- [Css](https://docs.rs/struct.Css.html)
- Represents a CSS class with a name, its style declarations, and optional pseudo rules.
- [Dynamic](https://docs.rs/struct.DynamicNode.html)- Node
- A closure-based dynamic node that re-renders when its dependency signals change.
- [Event](https://docs.rs/struct.EventAdapter.html)- Adapter
- Adapts various event value types into an `AttributeValue`for event attributes.
- [Event](https://docs.rs/struct.EventNamedAdapter.html)- Named - Adapter
- Adapts an event with a specific event name into an `AttributeValue`.
- [Hook](https://docs.rs/struct.HookContext.html)- Context
- Manages hook state across render cycles for a DynamicNode.
- [Interval](https://docs.rs/struct.IntervalHandle.html)- Handle
- A handle to a browser interval timer created by `use_interval`.
- [Media](https://docs.rs/struct.MediaRule.html)- Rule
- Represents a CSS @media rule attached to a class.
- [Native](https://docs.rs/struct.NativeEventHandler.html)- Event - Handler
- A wrapper around an event callback.
- [Pseudo](https://docs.rs/struct.PseudoRule.html)- Rule
- Represents a CSS pseudo-class or pseudo-element rule attached to a class.
- [Signal](https://docs.rs/struct.Signal.html)
- A reactive signal handle.
- [Signal](https://docs.rs/struct.SignalCell.html)- Cell
- A `Sync`wrapper for single-threaded global`Signal`access.
- [Text](https://docs.rs/struct.TextNode.html)- Node
- Represents a text node in the virtual DOM.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Attribute](https://docs.rs/enum.AttributeValue.html)- Value
- Represents the value of an HTML attribute.
- [Tag](https://docs.rs/enum.Tag.html)
- Represents the type of an HTML tag or a component.
- [Virtual](https://docs.rs/enum.VirtualNode.html)- Node
- Represents a node in the virtual DOM tree.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [batch](https://docs.rs/fn.batch.html)
- Batches signal updates within a closure, deferring DOM dispatch until the outermost batch completes.
- [mount](https://docs.rs/fn.mount.html)
- Mounts the given virtual DOM tree to a specific element matched by a CSS selector.
- [schedule_](https://docs.rs/fn.schedule_update.html)- update
- Schedules a deferred signal update with precise dirty marking.
- [use_](https://docs.rs/fn.use_cleanup.html)- cleanup
- Registers a cleanup callback that will be executed when the current
hook context is cleared (e.g., when a `match`arm switches).
- [use_](https://docs.rs/fn.use_interval.html)- interval
- Creates a recurring interval that invokes the given closure at the
specified period, returning an `IntervalHandle`that is automatically cleared when the hook context is cleared (i.e., when the component unmounts or a`match`arm switches).
- [use_](https://docs.rs/fn.use_signal.html)- signal
- Creates a new reactive signal with the given initial value.
- [use_](https://docs.rs/fn.use_window_event.html)- window_ - event
- Registers a `window.addEventListener`callback using event delegation, automatically removed when the hook context is cleared.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [component](https://docs.rs/attr.component.html)
- The `component`attribute macro for marking component functions.

## Expand description

euv CLI

The official CLI tool for the euv UI framework, providing run/build/fmt modes with hot reload and wasm-pack integration.

# synth-verify - Formal Verification for Synth Compiler

Formal verification infrastructure for the Synth WebAssembly-to-ARM compiler using SMT-based translation validation.

## Overview

This crate provides:

- **SMT-based translation validation**using Z3 SMT solver
- **Formal semantics**for WebAssembly and ARM operations
- **Property-based testing**framework with proptest
- **Automated verification**of synthesis rules

## Architecture

```
synth-verify/
├── wasm_semantics.rs      # WASM → SMT encoding (25+ operations)
├── arm_semantics.rs       # ARM → SMT encoding (processor state model)
├── translation_validator.rs # Equivalence prover (Alive2-inspired)
└── properties.rs          # Property-based tests (50+ properties)
```
## Usage

### Verifying a Synthesis Rule

```
use ;
use ;
// Create Z3 context
let ctx = create_z3_context;
let validator = new;
// Define a synthesis rule
let rule = SynthesisRule ;
// Verify the rule
match validator.verify_rule
```
### Batch Verification

```
// Verify multiple rules
let rules = vec!;
let results = validator.verify_rules;
for  in results
```
### Property-Based Testing

```
use CompilerProperties;
use *;
proptest!
```
## Verification Approach

### Translation Validation

For each synthesis rule `WASM_OP → ARM_OPS`, we prove:

```
∀inputs. ⟦WASM_OP⟧(inputs) = ⟦ARM_OPS⟧(inputs)
```
Using SMT solver:

- Create symbolic inputs
- Encode WASM semantics: `φ_wasm`
- Encode ARM semantics: `φ_arm`
- Assert: `φ_wasm ≠ φ_arm`
- Check satisfiability:
- **UNSAT**→ Proven correct
- **SAT**→ Counterexample found
- **UNKNOWN**→ Timeout

### Example: ADD Verification

```
; Symbolic inputs
(declare-const a (_ BitVec 32))
(declare-const b (_ BitVec 32))
; WASM: i32.add
(define-fun wasm-add () (_ BitVec 32)
  (bvadd a b))
; ARM: ADD R0, R0, R1
(define-fun arm-add () (_ BitVec 32)
  (bvadd a b))
; Prove equivalence
(assert (not (= wasm-add arm-add)))
(check-sat)  ; Returns: unsat → Proven!
```
## Verified Operations

| Operation | Status | Method |
|---|---|---|
| i32.add | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.sub | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.mul | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.div_s | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.div_u | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.and | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.or | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.xor | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.shl | ⚠ Partial | Complex |
| i32.shr_u | ⚠ Partial | Complex |
| i32.shr_s | ⚠ Partial | Complex |

## Dependencies

### Required

- **z3**- Z3 SMT solver Rust bindings (v0.12)
- **synth-synthesis**- Synthesis rules and operations
- **proptest**- Property-based testing

### System Requirements

Z3 requires either:

- System installation: `libz3-dev`or`z3`package
- Static linking: Built automatically (requires C++ compiler)

For development without Z3:

```
# Skip tests that require Z3
```
## Testing

```
# Run all tests (requires Z3)
# Run specific test suites
# Property-based testing with more cases
PROPTEST_CASES=10000
```
## Performance

- Verification time: 50-500ms per rule (SMT solving)
- Memory usage: ~50MB (Z3 context)
- Scalability: Linear in number of rules

## Limitations

- **Shift operations**: Modulo handling complex for SMT
- **Control flow**: Branch verification requires extended modeling
- **Memory operations**: Requires memory model formalization
- **Floating point**: Not yet supported

## Future Work

### Phase 1: Complete SMT Coverage

- Shift operation verification
- Control flow (branches, conditions)
- Memory operations (load/store)

### Phase 2: Optimization Verification

- DCE, constant folding, CSE correctness
- Loop optimization soundness
- Register allocation preservation

### Phase 3: Mechanized Proofs

- Port to Coq proof assistant
- Machine-checked correctness
- Certified synthesis rule library

## References

- **Alive2**: Automated LLVM verification (Lopes et al., PLDI 2021)
- **CompCert**: Verified C compiler (Leroy, POPL 2006)
- **VeriISLE**: Verified instruction selection (Nandi et al., PLDI 2020)
- **Z3**: Efficient SMT solver (de Moura & Bjørner, TACAS 2008)

## License

Dual-licensed under Apache-2.0 OR MIT

## Authors

PulseEngine Team

# thingd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/thingd/0.47.0/thingd/

## Expand description

Core primitives for thingd.

This crate owns the durable engine boundary: object storage, append-only
events, and queue storage. The default implementation is in-memory, with a
feature-gated `SQLite` adapter available for durable object, event, and
queue storage.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

| Feature | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `sqlite` | No | Enables with FTS5 search, WAL mode, and auto-migration`SqliteThingStore` |
| `connectors` | No | Enables CSV/JSON file connectors for data import |

[§](https://docs.rs#example-in-memory)Example (in-memory)

```
use thingd::{MemoryEngine, ObjectStore, EventLog, MemoryObject, MemoryEvent};
let mut engine = MemoryEngine::new();
let obj = MemoryObject::new("users", "alice", r#"{"name":"Alice"}"#);
engine.put_object(obj).unwrap();
let user = engine.get_object("users", "alice").unwrap();
assert_eq!(user.unwrap().body, r#"{"name":"Alice"}"#);
let event = MemoryEvent::new("audit", "user.created", r#"{"user":"alice"}"#);
engine.append_event(event).unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-sqlite--requires-sqlite-feature)Example (`SQLite` — requires `sqlite` feature)

```
#[cfg(feature = "sqlite")]
{
    use thingd::{SqliteThingStore, ObjectStore, MemoryObject};
    let mut db = SqliteThingStore::open_in_memory().unwrap();
    db.put_object(MemoryObject::new("users", "alice", r#"{"name":"Alice"}"#)).unwrap();
    let user = db.get_object("users", "alice").unwrap();
    assert_eq!(user.unwrap().body, r#"{"name":"Alice"}"#);
}
```

# num-order 1.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-order/1.2.0

Numerically consistent `Eq`, `Ord` and `Hash` implementations for various `num` types (`u32`, `f64`, `num_bigint::BigInt`, etc.).

# Example

```
use Ordering;
use Hasher;
use DefaultHasher;
use ;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// 40_000_000 can be exactly represented in f32, 40_000_001 cannot
// 40_000_001 becames 40_000_000.0 in f32
assert_eq!;
assert_ne!;
assert_eq!;
// same hash values are guaranteed for equal numbers
let mut hasher1 = new;
3u64.num_hash;
let mut hasher2 = new;
3.0f32.num_hash;
assert_eq!
```

# num_order - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-order/1.2.0/target-redirect/num_order/

## Expand description

`num-order` implements numerically consistent [Eq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Eq.html), [Ord](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html) and
[Hash](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.Hash.html) for various `num` types.

```
use std::cmp::Ordering;
use std::hash::Hasher;
use std::collections::hash_map::DefaultHasher;
use num_order::NumOrd;
assert!(NumOrd::num_eq(&3u64, &3.0f32));
assert!(NumOrd::num_lt(&-4.7f64, &-4i8));
assert!(!NumOrd::num_ge(&-3i8, &1u16));
// 40_000_000 can be exactly represented in f32, 40_000_001 cannot
// 40_000_001 becames 40_000_000.0 in f32
assert_eq!(NumOrd::num_cmp(&40_000_000f32, &40_000_000u32), Ordering::Equal);
assert_ne!(NumOrd::num_cmp(&40_000_001f32, &40_000_001u32), Ordering::Equal);
assert_eq!(NumOrd::num_partial_cmp(&f32::NAN, &40_000_002u32), None);
use num_order::NumHash;
// same hash values are guaranteed for equal numbers
let mut hasher1 = DefaultHasher::new();
3u64.num_hash(&mut hasher1);
let mut hasher2 = DefaultHasher::new();
3.0f32.num_hash(&mut hasher2);
assert_eq!(hasher1.finish(), hasher2.finish())
```
This crate can serve applications where [float-ord](https://crates.io/crates/float-ord),
[num-cmp](https://crates.io/crates/num-cmp), [num-ord](https://crates.io/crates/num-ord) are used.
Meanwhile it also supports hashing and more numeric types (`num-bigint`, etc.).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional Features

- `std`: enable std library
- `num-bigint`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-bigint::{BigInt, BigUint}`
- `num-rational`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-rational::Ratio<I>`, where- `I`can be- `i8`,- `i16`,- `i32`,- `i64`,- `i128`and- `isize`.- `Ratio<BigInt>`is supported when both- `num-bigint`and- `num-rational`is enabled
- `num-complex`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-complex::{Complex32, Complex64}`

# num_order - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-order/1.2.0/num_order/index.html

## Expand description

`num-order` implements numerically consistent [Eq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Eq.html), [Ord](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html) and
[Hash](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.Hash.html) for various `num` types.

```
use std::cmp::Ordering;
use std::hash::Hasher;
use std::collections::hash_map::DefaultHasher;
use num_order::NumOrd;
assert!(NumOrd::num_eq(&3u64, &3.0f32));
assert!(NumOrd::num_lt(&-4.7f64, &-4i8));
assert!(!NumOrd::num_ge(&-3i8, &1u16));
// 40_000_000 can be exactly represented in f32, 40_000_001 cannot
// 40_000_001 becames 40_000_000.0 in f32
assert_eq!(NumOrd::num_cmp(&40_000_000f32, &40_000_000u32), Ordering::Equal);
assert_ne!(NumOrd::num_cmp(&40_000_001f32, &40_000_001u32), Ordering::Equal);
assert_eq!(NumOrd::num_partial_cmp(&f32::NAN, &40_000_002u32), None);
use num_order::NumHash;
// same hash values are guaranteed for equal numbers
let mut hasher1 = DefaultHasher::new();
3u64.num_hash(&mut hasher1);
let mut hasher2 = DefaultHasher::new();
3.0f32.num_hash(&mut hasher2);
assert_eq!(hasher1.finish(), hasher2.finish())
```
This crate can serve applications where [float-ord](https://crates.io/crates/float-ord),
[num-cmp](https://crates.io/crates/num-cmp), [num-ord](https://crates.io/crates/num-ord) are used.
Meanwhile it also supports hashing and more numeric types (`num-bigint`, etc.).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional Features

- `std`: enable std library
- `num-bigint`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-bigint::{BigInt, BigUint}`
- `num-rational`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-rational::Ratio<I>`, where- `I`can be- `i8`,- `i16`,- `i32`,- `i64`,- `i128`and- `isize`.- `Ratio<BigInt>`is supported when both- `num-bigint`and- `num-rational`is enabled
- `num-complex`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-complex::{Complex32, Complex64}`

---

[50](https://docs.rs#50)/// Consistent comparison among different numeric types.
[51](https://docs.rs#51)pub trait NumOrd<Other> {
[52](https://docs.rs#52)    /// [PartialOrd::partial_cmp] on different numeric types
[53](https://docs.rs#53)    fn num_partial_cmp(&self, other: &Other) -> Option<Ordering>;
[54](https://docs.rs#54)
[55](https://docs.rs#55)    #[inline]
[56](https://docs.rs#56)    /// [PartialEq::eq] on different numeric types
[57](https://docs.rs#57)    fn num_eq(&self, other: &Other) -> bool {
[58](https://docs.rs#58)        matches!(self.num_partial_cmp(other), Some(Ordering::Equal))
[59](https://docs.rs#59)    }
[60](https://docs.rs#60)    #[inline]
[61](https://docs.rs#61)    /// [PartialEq::ne] on different numeric types
[62](https://docs.rs#62)    fn num_ne(&self, other: &Other) -> bool {
[63](https://docs.rs#63)        !self.num_eq(other)
[64](https://docs.rs#64)    }
[65](https://docs.rs#65)    #[inline]
[66](https://docs.rs#66)    /// [PartialOrd::lt] on different numeric types
[67](https://docs.rs#67)    fn num_lt(&self, other: &Other) -> bool {
[68](https://docs.rs#68)        matches!(self.num_partial_cmp(other), Some(Ordering::Less))
[69](https://docs.rs#69)    }
[70](https://docs.rs#70)    #[inline]
[71](https://docs.rs#71)    /// [PartialOrd::le] on different numeric types
[72](https://docs.rs#72)    fn num_le(&self, other: &Other) -> bool {
[73](https://docs.rs#73)        matches!(
[74](https://docs.rs#74)            self.num_partial_cmp(other),
[75](https://docs.rs#75)            Some(Ordering::Equal) | Some(Ordering::Less)
[76](https://docs.rs#76)        )
[77](https://docs.rs#77)    }
[78](https://docs.rs#78)    #[inline]
[79](https://docs.rs#79)    /// [PartialOrd::gt] on different numeric types
[80](https://docs.rs#80)    fn num_gt(&self, other: &Other) -> bool {
[81](https://docs.rs#81)        matches!(self.num_partial_cmp(other), Some(Ordering::Greater))
[82](https://docs.rs#82)    }
[83](https://docs.rs#83)    #[inline]
[84](https://docs.rs#84)    /// [PartialOrd::ge] on different numeric types
[85](https://docs.rs#85)    fn num_ge(&self, other: &Other) -> bool {
[86](https://docs.rs#86)        matches!(
[87](https://docs.rs#87)            self.num_partial_cmp(other),
[88](https://docs.rs#88)            Some(Ordering::Equal) | Some(Ordering::Greater)
[89](https://docs.rs#89)        )
[90](https://docs.rs#90)    }
[91](https://docs.rs#91)    #[inline]
[92](https://docs.rs#92)    /// [Ord::cmp] on different numeric types. It panics if either of the numeric values contains NaN.
[93](https://docs.rs#93)    fn num_cmp(&self, other: &Other) -> Ordering {
[94](https://docs.rs#94)        self.num_partial_cmp(other).unwrap()
[95](https://docs.rs#95)    }
[96](https://docs.rs#96)}
[97](https://docs.rs#97)

[99](https://docs.rs#99)///
[100](https://docs.rs#100)/// It's ensured that if `a.num_eq(b)`, then `a` and `b` will result in the same hash. Although the other direction is
[101](https://docs.rs#101)/// not ensured because it's infeasible, the hash function is still designed to be as sparse as possible.
[102](https://docs.rs#102)pub trait NumHash {
[103](https://docs.rs#103)    /// Consistent [Hash::hash][core::hash::Hash::hash] on different numeric types.
[104](https://docs.rs#104)    ///
[105](https://docs.rs#105)    /// This function will ensures if `a.num_eq(b)`, then `a.num_hash()` and `b.num_hash()` manipulate the state in the same way.
[106](https://docs.rs#106)    fn num_hash<H: Hasher>(&self, state: &mut H);

# NumHash in num_order - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-order/1.2.0/num_order/trait.NumHash.html

## Expand description

Consistent hash implementation among different numeric types.

It’s ensured that if `a.num_eq(b)`, then `a` and `b` will result in the same hash. Although the other direction is
not ensured because it’s infeasible, the hash function is still designed to be as sparse as possible.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

---

# num_order - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-order/latest/num_order/

## Expand description

`num-order` implements numerically consistent [Eq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Eq.html), [Ord](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html) and
[Hash](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.Hash.html) for various `num` types.

```
use std::cmp::Ordering;
use std::hash::Hasher;
use std::collections::hash_map::DefaultHasher;
use num_order::NumOrd;
assert!(NumOrd::num_eq(&3u64, &3.0f32));
assert!(NumOrd::num_lt(&-4.7f64, &-4i8));
assert!(!NumOrd::num_ge(&-3i8, &1u16));
// 40_000_000 can be exactly represented in f32, 40_000_001 cannot
// 40_000_001 becames 40_000_000.0 in f32
assert_eq!(NumOrd::num_cmp(&40_000_000f32, &40_000_000u32), Ordering::Equal);
assert_ne!(NumOrd::num_cmp(&40_000_001f32, &40_000_001u32), Ordering::Equal);
assert_eq!(NumOrd::num_partial_cmp(&f32::NAN, &40_000_002u32), None);
use num_order::NumHash;
// same hash values are guaranteed for equal numbers
let mut hasher1 = DefaultHasher::new();
3u64.num_hash(&mut hasher1);
let mut hasher2 = DefaultHasher::new();
3.0f32.num_hash(&mut hasher2);
assert_eq!(hasher1.finish(), hasher2.finish())
```
This crate can serve applications where [float-ord](https://crates.io/crates/float-ord),
[num-cmp](https://crates.io/crates/num-cmp), [num-ord](https://crates.io/crates/num-ord) are used.
Meanwhile it also supports hashing and more numeric types (`num-bigint`, etc.).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional Features

- `std`: enable std library
- `num-bigint`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-bigint::{BigInt, BigUint}`
- `num-rational`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-rational::Ratio<I>`, where- `I`can be- `i8`,- `i16`,- `i32`,- `i64`,- `i128`and- `isize`.- `Ratio<BigInt>`is supported when both- `num-bigint`and- `num-rational`is enabled
- `num-complex`: Support comparing against and hashing- `num-complex::{Complex32, Complex64}`

# num-bigint 0.4.7 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-bigint/^0.4.0

# num-bigint

Big integer types for Rust, `BigInt` and `BigUint`.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
```
## Features

The `std` crate feature is enabled by default, and is mandatory before Rust
1.36 and the stabilized `alloc` crate.  If you depend on `num-bigint` with
`default-features = false`, you must manually enable the `std` feature yourself
if your compiler is not new enough.

### Random Generation

`num-bigint` supports the generation of random big integers when the `rand`
feature is enabled. To enable it include rand as

```
 = "0.8"
 = {  = "0.4",  = ["rand"] }
```
Note that you must use the version of `rand` that `num-bigint` is compatible
with: `0.8`.

## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num-bigint` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## Alternatives

While `num-bigint` strives for good performance in pure Rust code, other
crates may offer better performance with different trade-offs.  The following
table offers a brief comparison to a few alternatives.

| Crate | License | Min rustc | Implementation | Features |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `num-bigint` | MIT OR Apache-2.0 | 1.60 | pure rust | dynamic width, number theoretical functions |
| `awint` | MIT OR Apache-2.0 | 1.70 | pure rust | fixed width, heap or stack, concatenation macros |
| `bnum` | MIT OR Apache-2.0 | 1.87 | pure rust | fixed width, parity with Rust primitives including floats |
| `crypto-bigint` | MIT OR Apache-2.0 | 1.85 | pure rust | fixed width, stack only |
| `ibig` | MIT OR Apache-2.0 | 1.49 | pure rust | dynamic width, number theoretical functions |
| `rug` | LGPL-3.0+ | 1.85 | bundles [GMP](https://gmplib.org/)via`gmp-mpfr-sys` | all the features of GMP, MPFR, and MPC |

## License

Licensed under either of

at your option.

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# num-complex 0.4.6 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-complex/^0.4.0

# num-complex

`Complex` numbers for Rust.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
```
## Features

This crate can be used without the standard library (`#![no_std]`) by disabling
the default `std` feature. Use this in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
 = false
```
Features based on `Float` types are only available when `std` or `libm` is
enabled. Where possible, `FloatCore` is used instead.  Formatting complex
numbers only supports format width when `std` is enabled.

## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num-complex` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## License

Licensed under either of

at your option.

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# num-modular 0.6.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-modular/^0.6.1

# num-modular

A generic implementation of integer division and modular arithmetics in Rust. It provide basic operators and an type to represent integers in a modulo ring. Specifically the following features are supported:

- Common modular arithmetics: `add`,`sub`,`mul`,`div`,`neg`,`double`,`square`,`inv`,`pow`
- Optimized modular arithmetics in **Montgomery form**
- Optimized modular arithmetics with **pseudo Mersenne primes**as moduli
- Optimized modular arithmetics with **trinomial Solinas primes**as moduli
- Fast **integer divisibility**check
- **Legendre**,- **Jacobi**and- **Kronecker**symbols

It also support various integer type backends, including primitive integers and `num-bigint`. Note that this crate also supports `[no_std]`. To enable `std` related functionalities, enable the `std` feature of the crate.

---

# num-rational 0.4.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-rational/^0.4.0

# num-rational

Generic `Rational` numbers (aka fractions) for Rust.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
```
## Features

This crate can be used without the standard library (`#![no_std]`) by disabling
the default `std` feature.  Use this in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
 = false
```
## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num-rational` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

# num-traits 0.2.19 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-traits/^0.2.0

# num-traits

Numeric traits for generic mathematics in Rust.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
```
## Features

This crate can be used without the standard library (`#![no_std]`) by disabling
the default `std` feature. Use this in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
 = false
# features = ["libm"]    # <--- Uncomment if you wish to use `Float` and `Real` without `std`
```
The `Float` and `Real` traits are only available when either `std` or `libm` is enabled.

The `FloatCore` trait is always available.  `MulAdd` and `MulAddAssign` for `f32`
and `f64` also require `std` or `libm`, as do implementations of signed and floating-
point exponents in `Pow`.

## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num-traits` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## License

Licensed under either of

at your option.

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# num-order 1.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-order/1.1.0

Numerically consistent `Eq`, `Ord` and `Hash` implementations for various `num` types (`u32`, `f64`, `num_bigint::BigInt`, etc.).

# Example

```
use Ordering;
use Hasher;
use DefaultHasher;
use ;
assert!;
assert!;
assert!;
// 40_000_000 can be exactly represented in f32, 40_000_001 cannot
// 40_000_001 becames 40_000_000.0 in f32
assert_eq!;
assert_ne!;
assert_eq!;
// same hash values are guaranteed for equal numbers
let mut hasher1 = new;
3u64.num_hash;
let mut hasher2 = new;
3.0f32.num_hash;
assert_eq!
```

---

# num-order 1.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-order/latest/source/CHANGELOG.md

#Changelog
##[1.2.0] - 2023-08-30
-Bump the version of `num-modular` to prevent a bug.
- The hash values of negative infinity and NaN are changed.
- The hash values of rationals with a multiple of M127 are changed.
> It's not released as a new major version because the previously designed values are not intended. It's set by mistake.
##[1.1.0] - 2023-08-29
Now the crate `num-traits` is an optional dependency, and the `libm` dependency is removed. The dependency version of `num-modular` is updated to v0.6.
##[1.0.4] - 2022-05-23
Bump the version of dependency `num-modular`.
##[1.0.3] - 2022-04-17
Bump the version of dependency `num-modular`.
##[1.0.2] - 2022-04-06
Bump the version of dependency `num-modular`, use `MersenneInt` for more efficient hashing.
##[1.0.1] - 2022-03-31
First public stable version of `num-order`! Numerical consistant order and hash comparison are fully supported for following types:
-Unsigned integers: `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `u128`- Signed integers: `i8`, `i16`, `i32`, `i64`, `i128`- Float numbers: `f32`, `f64`- (`num-rational`) Rational numbers: `Ratio<i8>`, `Ratio<i16>`, `Ratio<i32>`, `Ratio<i64>`, `Ratio<i128>`- (`num-complex`) Complex numbers: `Complex<f32>`, `Complex<f64>`> v1.0.0 was yanked because `num-rational` is accidentally added as default feature.

---

# num-order 1.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-order/latest/source/README.md

```
Numerically consistent `Eq`, `Ord` and `Hash` implementations for various `num` types (`u32`, `f64`, `num_bigint::BigInt`, etc.).
```rust
use std::cmp::Ordering;
use std::hash::Hasher;
use std::collections::hash_map::DefaultHasher;
use num_order::{NumOrd, NumHash};
assert!(NumOrd::num_eq(&3u64, &3.0f32));
assert!(NumOrd::num_lt(&-4.7f64, &-4i8));
assert!(!NumOrd::num_ge(&-3i8, &1u16));
// 40_000_000 can be exactly represented in f32, 40_000_001 cannot
// 40_000_001 becames 40_000_000.0 in f32
assert_eq!(NumOrd::num_cmp(&40_000_000f32, &40_000_000u32), Ordering::Equal);
assert_ne!(NumOrd::num_cmp(&40_000_001f32, &40_000_001u32), Ordering::Equal);
assert_eq!(NumOrd::num_partial_cmp(&f32::NAN, &40_000_002u32), None);
// same hash values are guaranteed for equal numbers
let mut hasher1 = DefaultHasher::new();
3u64.num_hash(&mut hasher1);
let mut hasher2 = DefaultHasher::new();
3.0f32.num_hash(&mut hasher2);
assert_eq!(hasher1.finish(), hasher2.finish())
```
```

---

# num-bigint 0.4.7 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-bigint/0.4.7

# num-bigint

Big integer types for Rust, `BigInt` and `BigUint`.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
```
## Features

The `std` crate feature is enabled by default, and is mandatory before Rust
1.36 and the stabilized `alloc` crate.  If you depend on `num-bigint` with
`default-features = false`, you must manually enable the `std` feature yourself
if your compiler is not new enough.

### Random Generation

`num-bigint` supports the generation of random big integers when the `rand`
feature is enabled. To enable it include rand as

```
 = "0.8"
 = {  = "0.4",  = ["rand"] }
```
Note that you must use the version of `rand` that `num-bigint` is compatible
with: `0.8`.

## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num-bigint` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## Alternatives

While `num-bigint` strives for good performance in pure Rust code, other
crates may offer better performance with different trade-offs.  The following
table offers a brief comparison to a few alternatives.

| Crate | License | Min rustc | Implementation | Features |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `num-bigint` | MIT OR Apache-2.0 | 1.60 | pure rust | dynamic width, number theoretical functions |
| `awint` | MIT OR Apache-2.0 | 1.70 | pure rust | fixed width, heap or stack, concatenation macros |
| `bnum` | MIT OR Apache-2.0 | 1.87 | pure rust | fixed width, parity with Rust primitives including floats |
| `crypto-bigint` | MIT OR Apache-2.0 | 1.85 | pure rust | fixed width, stack only |
| `ibig` | MIT OR Apache-2.0 | 1.49 | pure rust | dynamic width, number theoretical functions |
| `rug` | LGPL-3.0+ | 1.85 | bundles [GMP](https://gmplib.org/)via`gmp-mpfr-sys` | all the features of GMP, MPFR, and MPC |

## License

Licensed under either of

at your option.

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

## Expand description

The `Arbitrary` trait crate.

This trait provides an [ Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html) trait to
produce well-typed, structured values, from raw, byte buffers. It is
generally intended to be used with fuzzers like AFL or libFuzzer. See the

[trait’s documentation for details on automatically deriving, implementing, and/or using the trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
