# num_bigint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-bigint/^0.4.3/

## Expand description

Big Integer Types for Rust

- A `BigUint`
- A `BigInt``BigUint``Sign`

Common numerical operations are overloaded, so we can treat them the same way we treat other numbers.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use num_bigint::BigUint;
use num_traits::One;
// Calculate large fibonacci numbers.
fn fib(n: usize) -> BigUint {
    let mut f0 = BigUint::ZERO;
    let mut f1 = BigUint::ONE;
    for _ in 0..n {
        let f2 = f0 + &f1;
        f0 = f1;
        f1 = f2;
    }
    f0
}
// This is a very large number.
println!("fib(1000) = {}", fib(1000));
```
It’s easy to generate large random numbers:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use num_bigint::{ToBigInt, RandBigInt};
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let a = rng.gen_bigint(1000);
let low = -10000.to_bigint().unwrap();
let high = 10000.to_bigint().unwrap();
let b = rng.gen_bigint_range(&low, &high);
// Probably an even larger number.
println!("{}", a * b);
```
See the “Features” section for instructions for enabling random number generation.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

The `std` crate feature is enabled by default, which enables [ std::error::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html)
implementations and some internal use of floating point approximations. This can be disabled by
depending on

`num-bigint` with `default-features = false`. Either way, the `alloc` crate is
always required for heap allocation of the [/](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[digits.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#random-generation)Random Generation

`num-bigint` supports the generation of random big integers when the `rand`
feature is enabled. To enable it include rand as

```
rand = "0.8"
num-bigint = { version = "0.4", features = ["rand"] }
```
Note that you must use the version of `rand` that `num-bigint` is compatible
with: `0.8`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arbitrary-big-integers)Arbitrary Big Integers

`num-bigint` supports `arbitrary` and `quickcheck` features to implement
[ arbitrary::Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/arbitrary/1.4.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html) and

[, respectively, for both](https://docs.rs/quickcheck/1.0.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/quickcheck/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`quickcheck::Arbitrary`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[. These are useful for fuzzing and other forms of randomized testing.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#serialization)Serialization

The `serde` feature adds implementations of [ Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html) and

[for both](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)

`Deserialize`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[. Their serialized data is generated portably, regardless of platform differences like the internal digit size.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

The `num-bigint` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)
- A big signed integer type.
- [BigUint](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8.4/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

To get you started quickly, the easiest and highest-level way to get
a random value is to use [ random()](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html); alternatively you can use

[. The](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)

`thread_rng()`[trait provides a useful API on all RNGs, while the](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[and](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)

`distributions`[modules provide further functionality on top of RNGs.](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)

`seq````
use rand::prelude::*;
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    // Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
    println!("char: {}", rand::random::<char>());
}
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let y: f64 = rng.gen(); // generates a float between 0 and 1
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

- Generates a random value using the thread-local random number generator.
- [thread_](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)- rng - `std`and- `std_rng`
- Retrieve the lazily-initialized thread-local random number generator,
seeded by the system. Intended to be used in method chaining style,
e.g. `thread_rng().gen::<i32>()`, or cached locally, e.g.`let mut rng = thread_rng();`. Invoked by the`Default`trait, making`ThreadRng::default()`equivalent.

# num_modular - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-modular/0.6.4/target-redirect/num_modular/

## Expand description

This crate provides efficient Modular arithmetic operations for various integer types,
including primitive integers and `num-bigint`. The latter option is enabled optionally.

To achieve fast modular arithmetics, convert integers to any [ModularInteger](https://docs.rs/trait.ModularInteger.html) implementation
use static `new()` or associated [ModularInteger::convert()](https://docs.rs/trait.ModularInteger.html#tymethod.convert) functions. Some builtin implementations
of [ModularInteger](https://docs.rs/trait.ModularInteger.html) includes [MontgomeryInt](https://docs.rs/type.MontgomeryInt.html), [FixedMersenneInt](https://docs.rs/type.FixedMersenneInt.html) and [FixedSolinasInt](https://docs.rs/type.FixedSolinasInt.html).

Example code:

```
use num_modular::{ModularCoreOps, ModularInteger, MontgomeryInt};
// directly using methods in ModularCoreOps
let (x, y, m) = (12u8, 13u8, 5u8);
assert_eq!(x.mulm(y, &m), x * y % m);
// convert integers into ModularInteger
let mx = MontgomeryInt::new(x, &m);
let my = mx.convert(y); // faster than static MontgomeryInt::new(y, m)
assert_eq!((mx * my).residue(), x * y % m);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#comparison-of-fast-division--modular-arithmetics)Comparison of fast division / modular arithmetics

Several fast division / modulo tricks are provided in these crate, the difference of them are listed below:

- [PreModInv](https://docs.rs/struct.PreModInv.html): pre-compute modular inverse of the divisor, only applicable to exact division
- Barrett (to be implemented): pre-compute (rational approximation of) the reciprocal of the divisor, applicable to fast division and modulo
- [Montgomery](https://docs.rs/struct.Montgomery.html): Convert the dividend into a special form by shifting and pre-compute a modular inverse, only applicable to fast modulo, but faster than Barrett reduction
- [FixedMersenne](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedMersenne.html): Specialization of modulo in form- `2^P-K`under 2^127.
- [FixedTrinomialSolinas](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedTrinomialSolinas.html): Specialization of modulo in form- `2^P1-2^P2+K`under 2^127.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_fixed_monty_ops.html)- fixed_ - monty_ - ops
- Generates all `Reducer`methods except`new()`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedMersenne.html)- Mersenne
- A modular reducer for (pseudo) Mersenne numbers `2^P - K`as modulus.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedMersenne32.html)- Mersenne32
- A modular reducer for (pseudo) Mersenne numbers `2^P - K`as modulus with 32-bit operands.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedMersenne64.html)- Mersenne64
- A modular reducer for (pseudo) Mersenne numbers `2^P - K`as modulus with 64-bit operands.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedMontgomery32.html)- Montgomery32
- A modular reducer based on [Montgomery form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_modular_multiplication#Montgomery_form)for 32-bit operands, with the modulus`P`known at compile time.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedMontgomery64.html)- Montgomery64
- A modular reducer based on [Montgomery form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_modular_multiplication#Montgomery_form)for 64-bit operands, with the modulus`P`known at compile time.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedProth.html)- Proth
- A modular reducer for Proth primes `K * 2^N + 1`.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedProth32.html)- Proth32
- A modular reducer for Proth primes `K * 2^N + 1`with 32-bit operands.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedProth64.html)- Proth64
- A modular reducer for Proth primes `K * 2^N + 1`with 64-bit operands.

- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedTrinomialSolinas32.html)- Trinomial - Solinas32

- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedTrinomialSolinas64.html)- Trinomial - Solinas64
- A modular reducer for trinomial Solinas numbers `2^P1 - 2^P2 + K`as modulus with 64-bit operands.

- A modular reducer based on [Montgomery form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_modular_multiplication#Montgomery_form), only supports odd modulus.
- [Normalized2by1](https://docs.rs/struct.Normalized2by1Divisor.html)- Divisor
- Divide a DoubleWord by a prearranged divisor.

- A wrapper of [Normalized3by2Divisor](https://docs.rs/struct.Normalized3by2Divisor.html)that can be used as a[Reducer](https://docs.rs/trait.Reducer.html)
- [Reduced](https://docs.rs/struct.ReducedInt.html)- Int
- An integer in a modulo ring
- [Vanilla](https://docs.rs/struct.Vanilla.html)
- A plain reducer that just use normal [Rem](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.Rem.html)operators. It will keep the integer in range [0, modulus) after each operation.
- [udouble](https://docs.rs/struct.udouble.html)
- A double width integer type based on the largest built-in integer type [umax](https://docs.rs/type.umax.html)(currently[u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u128.html)), and to support double-width operations on it is the only goal for this type.

# PreModInv in num_modular - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-modular/^0.6.1/struct.PreModInv.html

Struct PreModInv   Copy item path  Source  `pub struct PreModInv<T> {  }`Expand description Pre-computing the modular inverse for fast divisibility check.

This struct stores the modular inverse of a divisor, and a limit for divisibility check.
See https://math.stackexchange.com/a/1251328  for the explanation of the trick

Construct the preinv instance with raw values.

This function can be used to initialize preinv in a constant context, the divisor d
is required only for verification of d_inv and q_lim.

Construct the preinv instance with raw values.

Struct Montgomery  Copy item path  Source  `pub struct Montgomery<T> {  }`Expand description A modular reducer based on Montgomery form , only supports odd modulus.

The generic type T represents the underlying integer representation for modular inverse `-m^-1 mod R`,

# FixedMersenne in num_modular - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-modular/^0.6.1/struct.FixedMersenne.html

## Expand description

A modular reducer for (pseudo) Mersenne numbers `2^P - K` as modulus.

Supports `P` up to 128 and `K < 2^(P-1)`. All inputs and outputs are [umax](https://docs.rs/type.umax.html) (currently `u128`).

The `P` is limited to 128 so that overflow checks aren’t necessary. This covers all Mersenne
primes within the range of [umax](https://docs.rs/type.umax.html) (i.e. `u128`).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use num_modular::{FixedMersenne, Reducer, umax};
const P: u8 = 31;
const K: umax = 1;
let modulus = (1 << P) - K; // 2^31 - 1 (Mersenne prime)
let reducer = FixedMersenne::<P, K>::new(&modulus);
let a = reducer.transform(1000);
let b = reducer.transform(2000);
assert_eq!(reducer.residue(reducer.mul(&a, &b)), (1000 * 2000) % modulus);
```

# FixedTrinomialSolinas in num_modular - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-modular/^0.6.1/struct.FixedTrinomialSolinas.html

## Expand description

A modular reducer for trinomial Solinas numbers `2^P1 - 2^P2 + K` as modulus.

Supports `P1` up to 127, `P2 < P1`, and odd signed `K` with `|K| < 2^P2`. All inputs and outputs are [umax](https://docs.rs/type.umax.html) (currently `u128`).

The `P1` is limited to 127 so that overflow checks aren’t necessary. This covers all trinomial
Solinas primes within the range of [umax](https://docs.rs/type.umax.html) (i.e. `u128`).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use num_modular::{FixedTrinomialSolinas, Reducer};
const P1: u8 = 31;
const P2: u8 = 13;
const K: i128 = 1;
let modulus = (1u128 << P1) - (1u128 << P2) + (K as u128);
let reducer = FixedTrinomialSolinas::<P1, P2, K>::new(&modulus);
let a = reducer.transform(1000);
let b = reducer.transform(2000);
assert_eq!(reducer.residue(reducer.mul(&a, &b)), (1000u128 * 2000) % modulus);
```

# impl_fixed_monty_ops in num_modular - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-modular/^0.6.1/macro.impl_fixed_monty_ops.html

```
macro_rules! impl_fixed_monty_ops {
    ($T:ty, $D:ty, $r2:expr, primitive) => { ... };
    ($T:ty, $D:ty, $r2:expr, udouble) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Generates all `Reducer` methods except `new()`.

The caller must provide an inherent `fn reduce(&self, monty: $D) -> $T`
and the associated constants `MODULUS` / `R2`.

# FixedMersenne32 in num_modular - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-modular/^0.6.1/struct.FixedMersenne32.html

## Expand description

A modular reducer for (pseudo) Mersenne numbers `2^P - K` as modulus with 32-bit operands.

Supports `P` up to 32 and `K < 2^(P-1)`. All inputs and outputs are `u32`.
The modulus `2^P - K` must be prime for modular inverse and Fermat-based operations to be valid.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use num_modular::{FixedMersenne32, Reducer};
const P: u8 = 13;
const K: u32 = 1;
let modulus = (1u32 << P) - K; // 2^13 - 1 = 8191 (Mersenne prime)
let reducer = FixedMersenne32::<P, K>::new(&modulus);
let a = reducer.transform(100);
let b = reducer.transform(200);
assert_eq!(reducer.residue(reducer.add(&a, &b)), 300 % modulus);
```

# FixedMersenne64 in num_modular - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-modular/^0.6.1/struct.FixedMersenne64.html

## Expand description

A modular reducer for (pseudo) Mersenne numbers `2^P - K` as modulus with 64-bit operands.

Supports `P` up to 64 and `K < 2^(P-1)`. All inputs and outputs are `u64`.
Uses `u128` as the double-width intermediate for multiplication and reduction.
The modulus `2^P - K` must be prime for modular inverse and Fermat-based operations to be valid.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use num_modular::{FixedMersenne64, Reducer};
const P: u8 = 61;
const K: u64 = 1;
let modulus = (1u64 << P) - K; // 2^61 - 1 (Mersenne prime)
let reducer = FixedMersenne64::<P, K>::new(&modulus);
let a = reducer.transform(1000);
let b = reducer.transform(2000);
assert_eq!(reducer.residue(reducer.mul(&a, &b)), (1000u64 * 2000) % modulus);
```

# FixedProth in num_modular - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-modular/^0.6.1/struct.FixedProth.html

## Expand description

A modular reducer for Proth primes `K * 2^N + 1`.

Supports `N` up to 127, `K` odd with `K < 2^N`.  Montgomery form with `R = 2¹²⁸`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use num_modular::{FixedProth, Reducer};
const N: u8 = 16;
const K: u8 = 1;
let modulus = (K as u128) * (1u128 << N) + 1; // 2^16 + 1 = 65537
let reducer = FixedProth::<N, K>::new(&modulus);
let a = reducer.transform(1000);
let b = reducer.transform(2000);
assert_eq!(reducer.residue(reducer.mul(&a, &b)), (1000u128 * 2000) % modulus);
```

# FixedProth32 in num_modular - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-modular/^0.6.1/struct.FixedProth32.html

## Expand description

A modular reducer for Proth primes `K * 2^N + 1` with 32-bit operands.

Supports `N` up to 31, `K` odd with `K < 2^N`.  Montgomery form with `R = 2³²`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use num_modular::{FixedProth32, Reducer};
const N: u8 = 4;
const K: u8 = 1;
let modulus = (K as u32) * (1u32 << N) + 1; // 1*2^4 + 1 = 17
let reducer = FixedProth32::<N, K>::new(&modulus);
let a = reducer.transform(3);
let b = reducer.transform(5);
assert_eq!(reducer.residue(reducer.add(&a, &b)), 8);
assert_eq!(reducer.residue(reducer.mul(&a, &b)), 15);
```

# FixedTrinomialSolinas32 in num_modular - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-modular/^0.6.1/struct.FixedTrinomialSolinas32.html

## Expand description

A modular reducer for trinomial Solinas numbers `2^P1 - 2^P2 + K` as modulus with 32-bit operands.

Supports `P1` up to 32, `P2 < P1`, and odd signed `K` with `|K| < 2^P2`. All inputs and outputs are `u32`.
The modulus `2^P1 - 2^P2 + K` must be prime for modular inverse and Fermat-based operations to be valid.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use num_modular::{FixedTrinomialSolinas32, Reducer};
const P1: u8 = 4;
const P2: u8 = 2;
const K: i32 = 1;
let modulus = (1u32 << P1) - (1u32 << P2) + (K as u32); // 2^4 - 2^2 + 1 = 13
let reducer = FixedTrinomialSolinas32::<P1, P2, K>::new(&modulus);
let a = reducer.transform(3);
let b = reducer.transform(5);
assert_eq!(reducer.residue(reducer.add(&a, &b)), 8);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# FixedTrinomialSolinas64 in num_modular - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-modular/^0.6.1/struct.FixedTrinomialSolinas64.html

## Expand description

A modular reducer for trinomial Solinas numbers `2^P1 - 2^P2 + K` as modulus with 64-bit operands.

Supports `P1` up to 64, `P2 < P1`, and odd signed `K` with `|K| < 2^P2`. All inputs and outputs are `u64`.
Uses `u128` as the double-width intermediate for multiplication and reduction.
The modulus `2^P1 - 2^P2 + K` must be prime for modular inverse and Fermat-based operations to be valid.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use num_modular::{FixedTrinomialSolinas64, Reducer};
const P1: u8 = 6;
const P2: u8 = 2;
const K: i64 = 1;
let modulus = (1u64 << P1) - (1u64 << P2) + (K as u64); // 2^6 - 2^2 + 1 = 61
let reducer = FixedTrinomialSolinas64::<P1, P2, K>::new(&modulus);
let a = reducer.transform(10);
let b = reducer.transform(20);
assert_eq!(reducer.residue(reducer.mul(&a, &b)), (10u64 * 20) % 61);
```

}## Expand description

A modular reducer that can ensure that the operations on integers are all performed in a modular ring.

Essential information for performing the modulo operation will be stored in the reducer.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

# udouble in num_modular - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-modular/^0.6.1/struct.udouble.html

## Expand description

A double width integer type based on the largest built-in integer type [umax](https://docs.rs/type.umax.html) (currently [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u128.html)), and
to support double-width operations on it is the only goal for this type.

Although it can be regarded as u256, it’s not as feature-rich as in other crates since it’s only designed to support this crate and few other crates (will be noted in comments).

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.hi)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.lo)

`lo: `[umax](https://docs.rs/type.umax.html)Least significant part

## Expand description

Math symbols related to modular arithmetics

Calculate Legendre Symbol (a|n), where a is `self`. Returns [None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) only if n is
not a prime.

Note that this function doesn’t perform a full primality check, since
is costly. So if n is not a prime, the result can be not reasonable.

[§](#panics)Panics

Only if n is not prime

Calculate Jacobi Symbol (a|n), where a is `self`. Returns [None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) if n is negative or even.

Calculate Kronecker Symbol (a|n), where a is `self`

Calculate Legendre Symbol (a|n), where a is `self`.

Note that this function doesn’t perform a full primality check, since
is costly. So if n is not a prime, the result can be not reasonable.

# num-rational 0.4.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-rational/0.4.2

# num-rational

Generic `Rational` numbers (aka fractions) for Rust.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
```
## Features

This crate can be used without the standard library (`#![no_std]`) by disabling
the default `std` feature.  Use this in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
 = false
```
## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num-rational` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## License

Licensed under either of

at your option.

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

- Ceiled integer division

- Floored integer division

- Simultaneous floored integer division and modulus

- Simultaneous integer division and modulus
- [gcd](https://docs.rs/fn.gcd.html)

- [gcd_lcm](https://docs.rs/fn.gcd_lcm.html)
- Calculates the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) and
Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) of the number and `other`.
- [lcm](https://docs.rs/fn.lcm.html)
- Calculates the Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) of the number and `other`.
- [mod_](https://docs.rs/fn.mod_floor.html)- floor
- Floored integer modulus
- [multinomial](https://docs.rs/fn.multinomial.html)
- Calculate the multinomial coefficient.
- [nth_](https://docs.rs/fn.nth_root.html)- root
- Returns the truncated principal `n`th root of an integer – see[Roots::nth_root](https://docs.rs/trait.Roots.html#tymethod.nth_root).
- [sqrt](https://docs.rs/fn.sqrt.html)
- Returns the truncated principal square root of an integer –
see [Roots::sqrt](https://docs.rs/trait.Roots.html#method.sqrt).

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Deserialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Serialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

# Ratio in num_rational - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-rational/^0.4.0/struct.Ratio.html

`pub struct Ratio<T> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Represents the ratio between two numbers.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_rational/lib.rs.html#128-130)#### pub fn [is_integer](https://docs.rs#method.is_integer)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_rational/lib.rs.html#128-130)

#### pub fn [is_integer](https://docs.rs#method.is_integer)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns true if the rational number is an integer (denominator is 1).

Returns a reduced copy of self.

In general, it is not necessary to use this method, as the only
method of procuring a non-reduced fraction is through `new_raw`.

**Panics if  denom is zero.**

Rounds to the nearest integer. Rounds half-way cases away from zero.

# num-traits 0.2.19 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-traits/0.2.19

# num-traits

Numeric traits for generic mathematics in Rust.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
```
## Features

This crate can be used without the standard library (`#![no_std]`) by disabling
the default `std` feature. Use this in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
 = false
# features = ["libm"]    # <--- Uncomment if you wish to use `Float` and `Real` without `std`
```
The `Float` and `Real` traits are only available when either `std` or `libm` is enabled.

The `FloatCore` trait is always available.  `MulAdd` and `MulAddAssign` for `f32`
and `f64` also require `std` or `libm`, as do implementations of signed and floating-
point exponents in `Pow`.

## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num-traits` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## License

Licensed under either of

at your option.

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

---

# autocfg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autocfg/^1/

## Expand description

A Rust library for build scripts to automatically configure code based on
compiler support.  Code snippets are dynamically tested to see if the `rustc`
will accept them, rather than hard-coding specific version support.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[build-dependencies]
autocfg = "1"
```
Then use it in your `build.rs` script to detect compiler features.  For
example, to test for 128-bit integer support, it might look like:

```
extern crate autocfg;
fn main() {
    let ac = autocfg::new();
    ac.emit_has_type("i128");
    // (optional) We don't need to rerun for anything external.
    autocfg::rerun_path("build.rs");
}
```
If the type test succeeds, this will write a `cargo:rustc-cfg=has_i128` line
for Cargo, which translates to Rust arguments `--cfg has_i128`.  Then in the
rest of your Rust code, you can add `#[cfg(has_i128)]` conditions on code that
should only be used when the compiler supports it.

[§](https://docs.rs#caution)Caution

Many of the probing methods of `AutoCfg` document the particular template they
use, **subject to change**. The inputs are not validated to make sure they are
semantically correct for their expected use, so it’s *possible* to escape and
inject something unintended. However, such abuse is unsupported and will not
be considered when making changes to the templates.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [AutoCfg](https://docs.rs/struct.AutoCfg.html)
- Helper to detect compiler features for `cfg`output in build scripts.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- A common error type for the `autocfg`crate.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [emit](https://docs.rs/fn.emit.html)
- Writes a config flag for rustc on standard out.
- [emit_](https://docs.rs/fn.emit_possibility.html)- possibility
- Indicates to rustc that a config flag should not generate an `unexpected_cfgs`warning
- [new](https://docs.rs/fn.new.html)
- Creates a new `AutoCfg`instance.
- [rerun_](https://docs.rs/fn.rerun_env.html)- env
- Writes a line telling Cargo to rerun the build script if the environment
variable `var`changes.
- [rerun_](https://docs.rs/fn.rerun_path.html)- path
- Writes a line telling Cargo to rerun the build script if `path`changes.

---

# Num in num_traits - Rust

```
pub trait Num:

```
[PartialEq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialEq.html)
    + [Zero](https://docs.rs/identities/trait.Zero.html)
    + [One](https://docs.rs/identities/trait.One.html)
    + [NumOps](https://docs.rs/trait.NumOps.html) {
    type [FromStrRadixErr](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.FromStrRadixErr);
    // Required method
    fn [from_str_radix](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_str_radix)(
        str: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
        radix: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html),
    ) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, Self::[FromStrRadixErr](https://docs.rs/trait.Num.html#associatedtype.FromStrRadixErr)>;
}## Expand description

The base trait for numeric types, covering `0` and `1` values,
comparisons, basic numeric operations, and string conversion.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_traits/lib.rs.html#95)#### fn [from_str_radix](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_str_radix)(str: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html), radix: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, Self::[FromStrRadixErr](https://docs.rs/trait.Num.html#associatedtype.FromStrRadixErr)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_traits/lib.rs.html#95)

#### fn [from_str_radix](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_str_radix)(str: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html), radix: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, Self::[FromStrRadixErr](https://docs.rs/trait.Num.html#associatedtype.FromStrRadixErr)>

Convert from a string and radix (typically `2..=36`).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use num_traits::Num;
let result = <i32 as Num>::from_str_radix("27", 10);
assert_eq!(result, Ok(27));
let result = <i32 as Num>::from_str_radix("foo", 10);
assert!(result.is_err());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#supported-radices)Supported radices

The exact range of supported radices is at the discretion of each type implementation. For
primitive integers, this is implemented by the inherent `from_str_radix` methods in the
standard library, which **panic** if the radix is not in the range from 2 to 36. The
implementation in this crate for primitive floats is similar.

For third-party types, it is suggested that implementations should follow suit and at least
accept `2..=36` without panicking, but an `Err` may be returned for any unsupported radix.
It’s possible that a type might not even support the common radix 10, nor any, if string
parsing doesn’t make sense for that type.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

Source: https://docs.rs/num-traits/^0.2.0/fn.clamp.html

`pub fn clamp<T: `[PartialOrd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html)>(input: T, min: T, max: T) -> T## Expand description

A value bounded by a minimum and a maximum

If input is less than min then this returns min. If input is greater than max then this returns max. Otherwise this returns input.

**Panics** in debug mode if `!(min <= max)`.

---
